nameStory: Summer savory earned its name from its peak growing season and its incredibly flavorful leaves that have been prized as a culinary herb for centuries. The word 'savory' comes from the Latin 'satureia,' referring to the plant's association with satyrs in Roman mythology, who were said to love its spicy fragrance. Unlike its perennial cousin winter savory, this annual herb completes its entire life cycle during the warm summer months.
description: Summer savory is a small, bushy annual herb that grows 1 to 2 feet tall with a delicate, upright appearance. Its slender bronze-green leaves are narrow and give off a wonderful spicy-sweet fragrance when crushed. From July through September, it produces tiny lilac-colored tubular flowers that attract bees and other small pollinators. This member of the mint family has a more refined look than many of its robust relatives, with an almost wispy growth habit.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Very narrow, slender leaves with a distinctive bronze-green color that feel smooth and release an intense, peppery-sweet aroma when rubbed between your fingers

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, tubular lilac or pale purple flowers clustered along the stems, each about 1/4 inch long with the irregular shape typical of mint family flowers

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Compact, bushy annual plant reaching 1-2 feet tall with multiple branching stems that give it a delicate, almost feathery appearance

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Square stems characteristic of the mint family, though more slender and refined than typical mints, with a slightly woody feel at the base

habitat: Summer savory is rarely found wild in New England, as it's primarily a cultivated garden herb that occasionally escapes or persists near old homesteads and herb gardens. When it does appear outside cultivation, look for it in well-drained, sunny spots with sandy or loamy soil. It thrives in disturbed areas with full sun exposure and doesn't compete well with aggressive native plants.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in late spring after soil warms. Young plants appear as small clusters of narrow, bronze-tinged leaves with square stems just emerging from the ground.
seasonality.summer: Peak identification time with full growth, aromatic leaves at their most fragrant, and lilac tubular flowers blooming from July through September. This is when the plant is most distinctive.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin to set seed and decline as temperatures drop. Leaves may turn more bronze or yellow, and the distinctive aroma becomes less intense as the annual completes its life cycle.
seasonality.winter: Completely absent as an annual plant. Only dried stems or scattered seeds remain where plants grew the previous summer.

funFact: Summer savory was so highly valued in medieval Europe that it was used as currency for paying rent and taxes, and Roman soldiers carried it in their field rations not just for flavor, but because they believed it gave them courage and strength in battle!
confusionNotes: Summer savory's narrow leaves and delicate appearance might be confused with young rosemary plants, but rosemary leaves are needle-like with white undersides and a completely different piney scent. Remember: savory smells spicy-sweet like pizza seasoning, while rosemary smells like Christmas trees.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse the culinary herb 'savory' with the word meaning flavorful but not sweet - they're related! This plant was so associated with good flavor that it gave us the culinary term. Summer savory is also sometimes called 'bean herb' because it's traditionally planted alongside beans in gardens.
compareHints: Since summer savory is the only member of its genus commonly found in New England, compare it to other small mint family herbs. Unlike spearmint or peppermint with their broad, toothed leaves, summer savory has extremely narrow, smooth-edged leaves. It's much more delicate than bee balm or other robust mints, and lacks the strong menthol scent of true mints, instead offering a warm, peppery fragrance.
